notes.front: What does a voltmeter measure?
notes.explanation: It is the instrument for measuring voltage, and it is connected in parallel with the component.
notes.example: To check the voltage across a lamp, connect a voltmeter across the lamp's two leads.

notes.front: What does an ammeter measure?
notes.explanation: It is the instrument for measuring current, and the current must flow through it.
notes.example: Compare a voltmeter, which measures voltage instead.

notes.front: What does an ohmmeter measure, and how?
notes.back: Resistance: it applies a small current and measures the resulting voltage.
notes.explanation: Resistance is voltage divided by current, so a known current and a measured voltage give the resistance.
notes.example: Compare an ammeter, which only measures current.

notes.front: What is a multimeter?
notes.back: An instrument that makes several measurements, including voltage and resistance.
notes.explanation: It can also be set to measure current; its setting must match what you are measuring.
notes.example: One meter used first as a voltmeter and then as an ohmmeter, by turning its selector.

notes.front: How is a voltmeter connected to measure the voltage applied to a component?
notes.explanation: Components in parallel always share the same voltage, so the meter reads the voltage across the component.

notes.front: How is a multimeter connected when it is set to measure current?
notes.explanation: Current is always the same through every component in series, so the meter carries the component's current.

notes.front: What precaution applies when measuring in-circuit resistance with an ohmmeter?
notes.back: Make sure the circuit is not powered.
notes.explanation: The ohmmeter works by supplying its own small current and measuring voltage, so the circuit must be off.

notes.front: What does an ohmmeter show when connected across a large, discharged capacitor?
notes.back: A resistance reading that increases with time.
notes.explanation: The meter's small current gradually charges the capacitor, so the reading climbs rather than staying steady.

notes.front: Which mistake can damage a multimeter?
notes.back: Trying to measure voltage while it is set to measure resistance.
notes.explanation: Check the selector before touching a live circuit: the setting must match the quantity you measure.

notes.front: Which type of solder should not be used for radio and electronic work?
notes.explanation: NASA's soldering standard for electrical connections calls for flux-cored solder with rosin flux and requires approval for any other flux. Rosin-core, lead-tin and tin-copper are the other types the pool lists; acid-core is the one to avoid.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7D08; NASA-STD-8739.3, Soldered Electrical Connections (Dec 1997), 3.1 and 6.11

notes.front: What does a cold tin-lead solder joint look like?
notes.explanation: NASA's soldering standard defines a cold solder connection as one with poor wetting and a grayish, porous appearance, caused by insufficient heat, inadequate cleaning or impurities in the solder, and lists it as a reason to reject a joint. A bright, shiny surface is not the sign.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7D09; NASA-STD-8739.3, Soldered Electrical Connections (Dec 1997), 3.1 and 6.11, 13.6

notes.front: How is a voltmeter connected to a component to measure applied voltage?
notes.explanation: Components in parallel share the same voltage, so a voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component.
notes.choices:
A) In series
B) In parallel
C) In quadrature
D) In phase
notes.choicesExplained: A: a series connection is for measuring current. C and D: "in quadrature" and "in phase" are not ways of connecting a meter.

notes.front: When configured to measure current, how is a multimeter connected to a component?
notes.explanation: Current is the same through every component in series, so a multimeter measuring current goes in series.
notes.choices:
A) In series
B) In parallel
C) In quadrature
D) In phase
notes.choicesExplained: B: a parallel connection is for measuring voltage. C and D: "in quadrature" and "in phase" are not ways of connecting a meter.

notes.front: Which instrument is used to measure electric current?
notes.explanation: An ammeter measures current, which must flow through it, so it is connected in series; an ohmmeter measures resistance and a voltmeter voltage.
notes.choices:
A) An ohmmeter
B) An electrometer
C) A voltmeter
D) An ammeter
notes.choicesExplained: A: an ohmmeter measures resistance. B: an electrometer is not the pool's instrument for current. C: a voltmeter measures electric potential (voltage).

notes.front: How does an ohmmeter measure the resistance of a circuit or component?
notes.back: By applying a small current and measuring the resulting voltage
notes.explanation: An ohmmeter applies a small current and measures the resulting voltage; resistance is voltage divided by current.
notes.choices:
A) By applying a small current and measuring the resulting voltage
B) By placing a variable resistor in parallel with the circuit
C) By placing a variable resistor in series with the circuit
D) By applying a variable voltage and measuring the resulting current change
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: an ohmmeter does not place a variable resistor in the circuit. D: it applies a current and measures voltage, not the other way round.

notes.front: Which of the following can damage a multimeter?
notes.back: Attempting to measure voltage when using the resistance setting
notes.explanation: On the resistance setting the meter supplies its own small current; connecting it across a live voltage is the mistake the pool says can damage it.
notes.choices:
A) Attempting to measure resistance using the voltage setting
B) Failing to connect one of the probes to ground
C) Attempting to measure voltage when using the resistance setting
D) Not allowing it to warm up properly
notes.choicesExplained: A: the reverse mistake is not the one the pool keys. B: the pool does not name a missing ground probe as a cause of damage. D: warming up is not the keyed risk.

notes.front: Which of the following measurements are made using a multimeter?
notes.explanation: A multimeter combines several meters in one: it can work as a voltmeter and as an ohmmeter, and it can be set to measure current. Voltage and resistance is the keyed pair.
notes.choices:
A) Signal strength and noise
B) Impedance and reactance
C) Voltage and resistance
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: signal strength and noise are not multimeter measurements. B: impedance and reactance are not what the pool keys. D: because A and B are wrong, "all" is wrong.

notes.front: Which of the following types of solder should not be used for radio and electronic applications?
notes.explanation: The pool keys acid-core solder as the type not to use; NASA's soldering standard for electrical connections calls for rosin flux instead and requires approval for any other flux.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7D08; NASA-STD-8739.3, Soldered Electrical Connections (Dec 1997), 3.1 and 6.11
notes.choices:
A) Acid-core solder
B) Lead-tin solder
C) Rosin-core solder
D) Tin-copper solder
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D: lead-tin, rosin-core and tin-copper solder are not the type the pool says to avoid; NASA's electronics soldering standard calls for flux-cored solder with rosin flux.

notes.front: What is the characteristic appearance of a cold tin-lead solder joint?
notes.explanation: NASA's soldering standard describes a cold solder connection as poorly wetted, grayish and porous, from insufficient heat, inadequate cleaning or impurities in the solder; the pool keys a rough or lumpy surface, not a bright or shiny one.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7D09; NASA-STD-8739.3, Soldered Electrical Connections (Dec 1997), 3.1 and 6.11
notes.choices:
A) Dark black spots
B) A bright or shiny surface
C) A rough or lumpy surface
D) A greenish tinge
notes.choicesExplained: A: dark black spots are not the keyed sign. B: a bright or shiny surface is not a cold joint. D: a greenish tinge is not the keyed sign.

notes.front: What reading indicates that an ohmmeter is connected across a large, discharged capacitor?
notes.explanation: The ohmmeter's small current slowly charges the capacitor, so the resistance reading increases with time.
notes.choices:
A) Increasing resistance with time
B) Decreasing resistance with time
C) Steady full-scale reading
D) Alternating between open and short circuit
notes.choicesExplained: B: the reading rises, not falls. C: it is not steady; it changes as the capacitor charges. D: it does not flip between open and short.

notes.front: Which of the following precautions should be taken when measuring in-circuit resistance with an ohmmeter?
notes.back: Ensure that the circuit is not powered
notes.explanation: Make sure the circuit is not powered: the ohmmeter supplies its own current.
notes.choices:
A) Ensure that the applied voltages are correct
B) Ensure that the circuit is not powered
C) Ensure that the circuit is grounded
D) Ensure that the circuit is operating at the correct frequency
notes.choicesExplained: A: there should be no applied voltage at all. C: grounding the circuit is not the precaution. D: the circuit should not be operating.

notes.front: Voltmeter or ammeter: which is connected in series, and which in parallel?
notes.back: Ammeter (or multimeter on current): in series. Voltmeter: in parallel.
notes.explanation: Series carries the same current; parallel shares the same voltage.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7D02, T7D03, T5D13, T5D14

notes.front: Ohmmeter or ammeter: which supplies its own small current, and which measures the current already flowing?
notes.back: Ohmmeter: supplies a small current. Ammeter: measures the circuit's current.
notes.explanation: That is why an ohmmeter is used on an unpowered circuit, while an ammeter needs the circuit working.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T7D05, T7D04, T7D11
